data.title: Alignment Healthcare Investigation Initiated: Kahn Swick & Foti, LLC Investigates the Officers and Directors of Alignment Healthcare, Inc. - ALHC
data.description:
Alignment Healthcare Investigation Initiated: Kahn Swick & Foti, LLC Investigates the Officers and Directors of Alignment Healthcare, Inc. - ALHC

Former Attorney General of Louisiana, Charles C. Foti, Jr., Esq., a partner at the law firm of Kahn Swick & Foti, LLC (“KSF”), announces that KSF has commenced an investigation into Alignment Healthcare, Inc. (“Alignment” or the “Company”) (NasdaqGS: ALHC).

On July 8, 2026, reports emerged that a former Alignment executive had filed a whistleblower lawsuit alleging that the Company deliberately misclassified $8 million to $10 million in routine operating expenses as capital expenditures to boost its stock price and executive compensation. According to the lawsuit, this maneuver artificially inflated the Company’s adjusted EBITDA and allowed it to report its “first full year of positive adjusted EBITDA as a public company.” Then, on September 15, 2026, at the Baird Global Healthcare Conference, Kao declined to comment on the Company’s Star Ratings positioning, stating, “I cannot talk about it at all[.]” On October 8, 2026, Alignment disclosed that CMS had downgraded the Star Rating for its H3815 contract to 3.5, making the plan ineligible for quality bonus payments in fiscal 2028. Following these disclosures, the Company’s share price declined precipitously.

KSF’s investigation is focusing on whether Alignment’s officers and/or directors breached their fiduciary duties to its shareholders or otherwise violated state or federal laws.

If you have information that would assist KSF in its investigation, or have been a long-term holder of Alignment shares and would like to discuss your legal rights, you may, without obligation or cost to you, call toll-free at 1-833-538-3606 or email KSF Managing Partner Lewis Kahn (lewis.kahn@ksfcounsel.com), or visit https://www.ksfcounsel.com/cases/nasdaqgs-alhc/ to learn more.

KSF, whose partners include former Louisiana Attorney General Charles C. Foti, Jr., is one of the nation’s premier boutique securities litigation law firms. KSF serves a variety of clients, including public and private institutional investors, and retail investors - in seeking recoveries for investment losses emanating from corporate fraud or malfeasance by publicly traded companies. KSF has offices in New York, Delaware, California, Louisiana, Chicago, and a representative office in Luxembourg.

data.title: KBRA Assigns Preliminary Ratings to Angel Oak Mortgage Trust 2026-6 (AOMT 2026-6)
data.description:
KBRA Assigns Preliminary Ratings to Angel Oak Mortgage Trust 2026-6 (AOMT 2026-6)

KBRA assigns preliminary ratings to ten classes of mortgage-backed certificates from Angel Oak Mortgage Trust 2026-6 (AOMT 2026-6), a $250.6 million non-prime RMBS transaction. The underlying collateral, comprised of 381 residential mortgages, and includes a meaningful concentration of collateral that KBRA considers to be “non-prime.” All the loans are either classified as non-qualified mortgages (62.8%) or exempt (37.2%) from the Ability-to-Repay/Qualified Mortgage rule due to being originated for non-consumer loan purposes. Angel Oak Mortgage Solutions originated 65.0% of the pool, with no other originator comprising over 10% of the collateral.

KBRA’s rating approach incorporated loan-level analysis of the mortgage pool through its Residential Asset Loss Model (REALM), an examination of the results from third-party loan file due diligence, cash flow modeling analysis of the transaction’s payment structure, reviews of key transaction parties and an assessment of the transaction’s legal structure and documentation. This analysis is further described in our U.S. RMBS Rating Methodology.

data.title: Nowhere to hide: Tech selloff hits software and chip stocks alike
data.description:
By Hannah Pedone

The software and semiconductor sectors haven't been trading in tandem much this year, but they collectively fell Friday as AI and interest-rate fears hit the market

Shares of Salesforce closed down 2% on Friday amid a broad-based selloff in the technology stocks.

Even the software sector wasn't immune from a broad-based technology selloff in the stock market Friday.

Investors had been rotating into the software sector earlier in the week, deeming these stocks to be compelling alternatives to highflying chip stocks that were seen as more vulnerable to concerns about the sustainability of artificial-intelligence spending.

But semiconductor and software stocks fell in tandem on Friday, leaving tech investors with nowhere to hide. The iShares Expanded Tech-Software Sector exchange-traded fund IGV, a proxy for the software sector, closed down 4.8%, while the iShares Semiconductor ETF SOXX was off 4.1%.

Within the software sector, ServiceNow's stock (NOW) finished down 4% and Oracle's stock (ORCL) closed 5% lower. Shares of Salesforce (CRM) lost 2% on the day, while Twilio's stock (TWLO) was the S&P 500's SPX biggest loser with its 10.6% decline.

D.A. Davidson analyst Gil Luria told MarketWatch that what used to be a negative correlation between chip stocks and software stocks is "no longer a major factor in the market." He said that Friday's broad-based technology selloff was "not leaving any stock untouched."

"Investors no longer view AI progress as bad for software and are treating individual software companies based on their specific prospects," he said.

Morningstar analyst Luke Yang told MarketWatch there wasn't one single factor gripping the market on Friday, as investors seemed to be digesting a broad breakdown of faith in the AI trade this week.

The "wide range of potential outcomes" for companies tied to the AI trade has made it difficult for investors to maintain faith in AI-exposed stocks, he said - whether it be the indebted neocloud provider CoreWeave (CRWV), chip giant like Nvidia (NVDA) or software and cloud company Oracle (ORCL).

Cybersecurity stocks were also caught up in the software selloff on Friday after Palo Alto Networks (PANW) - which sells firewall products to corporate customers - released an advisory disclosing a security vulnerability earlier this week. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which lies within the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, added Palo Alto Networks to its catalog of known security vulnerabilities.

The Amplify Cybersecurity ETF HACK closed down 4% on Friday, with Palo Alto Networks and CrowdStrike Holdings (CRWD) shares each falling more than 7%.

One issue could be the specter of interest-rate hikes, which affects technology companies across the board that have to borrow money.

The "data-center buildout requires capital which is becoming more expensive," Luria said, as higher rates mean higher funding costs for companies investing heavily in AI infrastructure.

Software stocks are also sensitive to rate hikes as their valuations are often tied to cash flows years into the future, and higher interest rates change the way those are valued. And many software companies need to borrow money as well.

Financial-technology stocks may be feeling the pain as well from fears of an imminent rate hike, as higher rates mean higher default risk for lenders, Mizuho anlayst Dan Dolev told MarketWatch.

Speaking Friday at the International Monetary Fund and World Bank Group's annual meeting in Bangkok, Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh declined to share any expectations for the central bank's upcoming rate-setting meeting.

See also: The murky AI milestone that has some of the industry's leading voices increasingly on edge

-Hannah Pedone

data.title: UL Solutions Warns of GFCI and Duplex Wall Outlets Modified by Third Parties to Include Built-in Cameras
data.description:
UL Solutions Warns of GFCI and Duplex Wall Outlets Modified by Third Parties to Include Built-in Cameras

After manufacturing, third parties added built-in cameras to the wall outlets; UL Solutions did not evaluate the modified products and recommends that they be immediately removed from service and discarded.

UL Solutions (NYSE: ULS), a global leader in applied safety science, issued a public notice regarding ground fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) and duplex wall outlets that were UL Certified by the original manufacturer and bear the UL Mark, but were subsequently modified by third parties to include hidden cameras in the construction.

This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261016283811/en/

UL Solutions issued a public notice regarding ground fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) and duplex wall outlets that were UL Certified by the original manufacturer and bear the UL Mark, but were subsequently modified by third parties to include hidden cameras in the construction.

The GFCI and duplex wall outlets employing cameras have not been evaluated by UL Solutions and are not authorized to bear the UL Mark when they employ cameras. UL Solutions does not certify GFCI or duplex outlets that include a hidden camera.

The GFCI or duplex wall outlets covered by this notice are sold under the product names “Hidden Surveillance Camera GFCI Wall Outlet, Spy Security Camera” and “Hidden Surveillance Camera Outlet, Spy Security Camera 20 Amp” on e-commerce platforms, including Amazon, in the United States. The affected GFCI and duplex wall outlets bear a “Merlan” brand sticker and employ camera components.

It is unknown whether the GFCI and duplex wall outlets employing cameras function as intended or comply with any safety requirements. It is unknown whether the GFCI and other safety features will operate as intended to mitigate an unsafe condition. UL Solutions recommends that these products be immediately removed from service and discarded.

Images of the GFCI and duplex wall outlets are available on UL.com: https://www.ul.com/news/ul-solutions-warns-gfci-and-duplex-wall-outlets-modified-third-parties-include-built-cameras.

data.title: The bond market shrugged off two inflation shocks. Why stock investors should pay attention.
data.description:
By Robert Ross

Hot CPI and PPI data should have pushed Treasury yields higher. Instead, bond buyers stepped in to suggest yields have risen high enough to become attractive for investors.

Bad news has stopped hurting bonds. Here's what that means for stock investors.

The bond market just shrugged off the kind of news that should have sent yields higher. Investors should take notice, as it could mean the top for yields is in.

For the past few months, the biggest threat hanging over markets has been the relentless rise in long-term Treasury yields. The 10-year yield BX:TMUBMUSD10Y recently touched 5.36%, its highest level in roughly 24 years, putting pressure on everything from mortgages to small-cap stocks. When yields rise, bond prices fall.

And then, inflation data gave bond bears exactly what they wanted. September's consumer-price index came in hotter than expected as headline inflation reached 3.7%, slightly above Wall Street's expectations. The immediate reaction was predictable: the 10-year Treasury yield jumped back toward 5.33%.

Then the unthinkable happened: Buyers showed up in droves as the 10-year quickly retreated to 5.18% by the end of Wednesday's session.

The following morning gave the bond market an even tougher test. Producer prices surged 1.3% in September, the largest monthly increase in more than four years and roughly twice what economists expected. If inflation was about to unleash another leg higher in Treasury yields, this was the kind of report that should have done it, as investors would price in even more interest-rate hikes from the Federal Reserve.

Instead, the 10-year yield plunged. By the end of the session, it had fallen roughly 10 basis points to 5.09%, its biggest one-day decline in more than a year. (One basis point is the same as 0.01 percentage point.)

That type of price action gets my attention.

When bad news stops hurting

The market does not ring a bell at the bottom. In October 2022, the bottom in stocks came when the S&P 500 SPX rallied after a similarly hot CPI print.

Just like then, the bad news kept coming, but prices stopped falling. In fact, they did the opposite of what conventional wisdom expects. When enough bad news is already baked into an asset's price, investor positioning can become so negative that even another ugly headline struggles to push it lower.

And I think we may be reaching that point in Treasurys, as after two hot inflation reports arrived within 48 hours, long-term yields headed lower.

There are other explanations for Thursday's rally. The selloff in AI stocks created safe-haven demand for government bonds, and comments from Federal Reserve officials reduced expectations for another immediate rate increase.

But that doesn't invalidate the signal. Treasurys had plenty of reasons to sell off - and yet they didn't.

Buyers are finally showing up

The inflation reaction is also part of a broader pattern.

A week earlier, the U.S. government auctioned $39 billion of 10-year Treasurys after yields had surged above 5.36%.

Demand was excellent. Investors submitted $2.77 in bids for every $1 of bonds available, while indirect bidders, a category that includes foreign institutions, absorbed more than 80% of the offering. Primary dealers were left with just 2.5%, their smallest share since the financial crisis.

There is a simple reason this may be happening: High yields eventually become the cure for high yields.

A 10-year Treasury yielding more than 5% starts looking awfully attractive to retirees, pension funds, insurers, foreign institutions and anyone else searching for dependable income.

Fund investors are noticing, too. Nearly $14 billion flowed into U.S. government-bond funds in early October following a record $59.3 billion during the third quarter.

Eventually, the yield gets high enough that investors stop asking how much further bond prices can fall and start asking how much they should buy.

We may be finding that level.

Why this matters for stocks

I'm not declaring that 5.36% was the exact top in the 10-year yield.

Bond volatility remains elevated. The MOVE Index - essentially the bond market's version of the Cboe Volatility Index VIX, which tracks volatility in the stock market - is still above 100 even after retreating from a recent peak around 114.

But the evidence is building: Strong auctions. Heavy fund inflows. Buyers appearing above 5.3%. And now, two inflation surprises that failed to restart the selloff.

A sustained peak in long-term yields would have consequences far beyond the Treasury market.

Mortgage rates could get some relief. Small companies would face less pressure from financing costs. Growth-stock valuations would get a friendlier discount rate. And investors buying Treasurys today could potentially collect 5%-plus income while also benefiting from capital appreciation if yields fall.

And if long-term yields really are topping, there are several ways investors can potentially profit from the reversal.

The easiest way is to buy long-duration Treasury ETFs like the iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF TLT, or high-yield plays with pipeline master limited partnerships like Enterprise Product Partners (EPD).

But I prefer vehicles that can move fast if we do get a reversal in rates. And in my next issue of Let's Analyze, I'll break down the leveraged Treasury trade I just added to my own portfolio to capitalize if yields continue falling. Click here to have the full report sent to your inbox when it goes live.

For now, it's important to pay attention to how bonds react to the news than to the news itself. We all know inflation is too high, the Fed has a difficult job and fiscal deficits aren't disappearing.

The bond market also knows all that. And it increasingly seems like prices may have more than reflected that reality.

Robert Ross is the founder of TikStocks and author of "A Beginner's Guide to High-Risk, High-Reward Investing." A former chief equity analyst at Mauldin Economics, Ross writes the investment newsletter Let's Analyze on Substack and hosts the weekly "Room to Run" podcast.

-Robert Ross
